fca2022.title: Final Notice: TSB Bank plc (Reference Number 191240)
fca2022.author: Financial Conduct Authority
fca2022.quote: Migration off the LBG IT Platform to Proteo4UK was irreversible, creating risk if any major issues arose.
quotes: 1.1 For the reasons given in this Final Notice, the Authority hereby imposes on TSB Bank plc (“TSB”) a financial penalty of £29.75 million pursuant to section 206 of the Act.

2.5 Over the weekend of 20 - 22 April 2018, TSB undertook the Main Migration Event (“MME”), during which it migrated the majority of the operations of its corporate systems, customer services and customer data to the new Proteo4UK Platform.

2.5 From an early point after the system went live on 22 April 2018, TSB encountered serious issues which significantly impacted the ability of some customers to access and use their account in the first few days after MME.
2.7 Overall, TSB did not return to a BAU position until 10 December 2018.

2.8 Between 22 April 2018 and 7 April 2019, TSB received 225,492 complaints from customers (c.4.3% of its customer base as at MME) as a result of the Migration Incident, and paid a total of £32,705,762 in redress during that period.

2.27 ...leading to a go-live launch following which, if a major incident occurred, TSB would be unable to roll back on to the LBG Platform and would be reliant on SABIS as its outsourced IT service provider to fix multiple technical incidents which could have a major impact on customers.
4.2 During the Relevant Period, it had approximately 5.2 million customers.
4.24 a) ... There was also an issue relating to 26 customers seeing other customers’ statements or communications through the “inbox” on the internet banking screen;
4.24 c) During the first week 20 – 30% of retail and business customers could not make any payments online, due to password errors and an inability to reset their credentials.

4.32 “Sabadell estimates that it can deliver, through the application of Sabadell’s skills and technology, efficiency cost savings in IT amounting to approximately £160 million per annum on a pre-tax basis, in the third full year after completion of the Offer. These expected savings derive from a full migration of the IT transitional services currently provided by Lloyds onto Sabadell’s proprietary Proteo technology platform.”
4.32 At the time of the offer, Sabadell had previously migrated seven banks on to its IT banking platform, Proteo, following their acquisition

4.40 It was stated that “The current plan is aspirational: it has been created to meet the deadlines for the Proteo build and the data migration in 2017. As such it has been created on a top-down and ‘right-to-left’ basis.”

4.48 Sabadell’s existing methodology for IT migrations was to use a ‘big bang’ or single operation data migration approach, under which all data would be migrated in a single main migration event weekend.
4.55 Migration off the LBG IT Platform to Proteo4UK was irreversible, creating risk if any major issues arose.
4.50 Sometimes, a firm will have a ‘roll-back’ plan, where, in the face of major problems, it can revert to the previous system. A ‘roll-back’ plan was not possible for TSB in these circumstances.

4.51 Under TSB’s arrangements, it was contractually required to notify LBG of its intentions to exit the agreement via migration (and thereby waive its right to the carve-out option which it would otherwise retain until 31 March 2019). Once it had done so, TSB would not be able to continue to use LBG’s platform long term. In addition, following the data migration there would be a very short window to stop the LBG IT Platform from being disabled. Consequently, after MME it was, technically speaking, essentially impossible to roll back from the changes made and revert to using the LBG IT Platform instead of Proteo4UK.

4.97 Testing of data migration was used to validate that data could be transferred from the LBG IT Platform to the Proteo4UK Platform... a) MACs – these tested the migrated data during the extract, transform and load process...; and b) Dress rehearsals – these were essentially MACs carried out in the timeframe that would be required for MME.
2.9 The direct causes of the technical problems experienced during the Migration Incident substantially related to issues with IT configuration, capacity and coding.

4.48 TSB opted for a predominantly single event data migration, although some functionality and data was migrated prior to the MME through Governed Transition Events (or “GTEs”) starting in 2017. These included the Faster Payments system, mobile app and ATMs.
[p.102, signature block] Kerralie Wallbridge / Head of Department / Financial Conduct Authority, Enforcement and Market Oversight Division
supports: MME weekend 20-22 April 2018; live 22 April 2018
approximately 5.2 million customers
migration was irreversible / no roll back on to the LBG Platform
20-30% of retail and business customers could not pay online in week one
26 customers saw other customers' statements
not back to BAU until 10 December 2018
225,492 complaints and GBP 32,705,762 redress
GBP 160 million per annum IT savings promised in the Sabadell Offer Document
plan 'created on a top-down and right-to-left basis'
Sabadell's method was 'big bang', a single main migration event weekend
FCA penalty GBP 29.75 million, dated 20 December 2022
a roll-back plan 'was not possible'; the bar was contractual - TSB had to waive the carve-out option to migrate, and the LBG platform would be disabled shortly after the data moved
the migration was 'predominantly' single-event: Faster Payments, the mobile app and ATMs moved earlier via GTEs from 2017
the extract/transform/load was re-run repeatedly through MAC cycles, MDT cycles and dress rehearsals
the direct causes of the incident were IT configuration, capacity and coding - not stale or mismatched migrated data
the Final Notice is signed by Kerralie Wallbridge, Head of Department, FCA Enforcement and Market Oversight Division - not by Mark Steward

fcapr2022.title: TSB fined £48.65m for operational resilience failings (press release)
fcapr2022.author: Financial Conduct Authority
fcapr2022.quote: The Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) and the Prudential Regulation Authority (PRA) have fined TSB Bank plc (“TSB”) a total of £48,650,000 for operational risk management and governance failures, including management of outsourcing risks, relating to the bank’s IT upgrade programme.
quotes: TSB was fined £29,750,000 by the FCA and £18,900,000 by the PRA.
While the data itself migrated successfully, the platform immediately experienced technical failures.

Mark Steward, FCA Executive Director of Enforcement and Market Oversight said: ‘The failings in this case were widespread and serious which had a real impact on the day-to-day lives of a significant proportion of TSB’s customers, including those who were vulnerable.’

‘The firm failed to plan for the IT migration properly, the governance of the project was insufficiently robust and the firm failed to take reasonable care to organise and control its affairs responsibly and effectively, with adequate risk management systems.’

However, the regulators’ found that TSB failed to organise and control the IT migration programme adequately, and it failed to manage the operational risks arising from its IT outsourcing arrangements with its critical third-party supplier.
All of TSB’s branches and a significant proportion of its 5.2 million customers were affected by the initial issues.
supports: combined FCA + PRA penalty of GBP 48,650,000
Mark Steward's title and quoted statement
the charge was planning and governance, not the outage itself
5.2 million customers, restated in the FCA's own summary of the incident
'While the data itself migrated successfully, the platform immediately experienced technical failures.'

unverified: Paul Pester's name, role and September 2018 resignation - the FCA and PRA Final Notices are anonymised and name no individual at TSB, and no primary source for the resignation could be opened. Not used in the prose.
Richard Meddings' name and role - same reason. Not used in the prose.

The often-quoted total cost figures of c.£330m of incident/remediation cost and £318m of migration spend, and the £107.4m statutory pre-tax loss for 2018 - these come from TSB's 2018 annual results, which could not be opened. Not used in the prose; the prose uses the £32,705,762 redress figure stated in the FCA Final Notice instead.
33,101 complaints in the first ten days and the '1,156% jump' - not stated in the FCA Final Notice, which gives 225,492 complaints over 22 April 2018 to 7 April 2019. Not used in the prose.
Fraud attacks peaking at c.70x normal about three weeks after migration - attributed to the Treasury Committee's HC 224 report, which returned HTTP 403 and could not be opened. Not used in the prose.

The Slaughter and May 'Independent Review of TSB's 2018 Migration' body text: the report PDF at tsb.co.uk/content/dam/tsb-public/documents/media-centre/Slaughter-and-May-final-report.pdf downloads (51MB) but carries no usable text layer, so nothing is quoted from the report itself and it is not cited.

Correction to the allocated brief, checked 2026-08-22: the brief dates the Slaughter and May review to 2022 and gives TSB 5.4 million customers. TSB's own news release (tsb.co.uk/news-releases/slaughter-and-may.html) dates the review 19 November 2019, and FCA Final Notice para 4.2 says 'approximately 5.2 million customers'. The verified figures are used in the prose.

REMOVED at verification 2026-08-22: 'Mark Steward signed TSB's Final Notice'. The notice is signed at p.102 by Kerralie Wallbridge, Head of Department, FCA Enforcement and Market Oversight Division. Steward is the FCA's quoted voice in the press release, not the signatory. Card p2c11-c1 now says only that the notice is dated 20 December 2022.

REMOVED at verification 2026-08-22: 'Going back meant discarding every real payment the new platform had already taken, so nobody went back' (prose) and 'reads and writes flipped together, which is what made it irreversible' (card p2c11-c4). Paras 4.50-4.51 give a contractual cause instead: TSB had to waive its carve-out right to migrate, and after the data moved there was 'a very short window to stop the LBG IT Platform from being disabled'. No ordering of deploys would have preserved a rollback.

REMOVED at verification 2026-08-22: 'Migrate: a one-shot copy instead of a resumable, re-runnable stream' (card p2c11-c4). Contradicted by paras 4.97 and 4.112(b) - MAC cycles, MDT cycles and dress rehearsals re-ran the extract/transform/load - and by the press release: 'While the data itself migrated successfully, the platform immediately experienced technical failures.' The data copy is the one part of TSB's migration that worked.

SCOPE FIX at verification 2026-08-22: the 225,492 complaints and £32,705,762 redress are counted over 22 April 2018 to 7 April 2019 (para 2.8), i.e. roughly four months past the 10 December 2018 return to BAU. The prose originally read 'not back to business as usual until 10 December, after 225,492 complaints...', placing the total before the date it postdates. Reworded to 'In the year from migration'.

NOT USED, checked 2026-08-22: 'no shadow reads / no mismatch metric' as a statement about TSB's verification generally. TSB ran extensive pre-migration data testing (MAC and MDT cycles, dress rehearsals); what it did not run is a live production window serving the old platform's answer while comparing the new one's. The prose claim is scoped to that narrow sense only.
